title: System Design Document
summary: Master System Design Document through explanation, prediction, implementation, and review.

challenges.title: Recall checkpoint
challenges.prompt: Without reopening the lesson, explain System Design Document in your own words. Include the problem it solves, the core mechanism, and one boundary or failure.
challenges.hint: Use “Problem and scope” as a cue, then close the lesson again.

challenges.title: Prediction checkpoint
challenges.prompt: Choose one example or source file from this mission. Predict its behavior for a normal input and a changed or invalid input before running or revealing the reference. Explain the rule separating the outcomes.
challenges.hint: Change one condition at a time so the result teaches a rule.

challenges.title: Build and prove checkpoint
challenges.prompt: Implement, debug, or adapt the mission exercise yourself. Record the acceptance criterion, command or interaction used to verify it, failure evidence, and one tradeoff. Do not paste the reference solution.
challenges.hint: A passing check, measured result, focused diff, or reproducible demo is stronger than ‘done.’

# System Design Document

## Problem and scope

- Primary users:
- Core use cases:
- Non-goals:
- Constraints:

## Quality requirements

Quantify availability, latency, durability, consistency, privacy, recovery,
and cost expectations where they influence design.

## Assumptions and estimates

Show units and arithmetic for traffic, concurrency, storage, bandwidth, and
growth. Label assumptions that need measurement.

## API and events

Define the important commands, queries, resources, event shapes, error
behavior, idempotency, pagination, and compatibility strategy.

## Data model

Describe ownership, keys, relationships, invariants, indexes, retention, and
transaction boundaries.

## Architecture and flows

Include one container diagram and sequence flows for the normal path and the
most important failure/retry path.

## Consistency and delivery guarantees

State what is strongly consistent, eventually consistent, ordered, at-most
once, or at-least once. Do not claim exactly once without defining the scope
and mechanism.

## Reliability

Cover timeouts, retries, backpressure, load shedding, graceful degradation,
recovery, backups, and disaster assumptions.

## Security and privacy

Identify assets, trust boundaries, authentication, authorization, encryption,
secret handling, abuse controls, audit needs, and retention.

## Observability

Define health signals, logs, metrics, traces, service objectives, and the
questions an operator must be able to answer.

## Alternatives and tradeoffs

Compare at least two credible options plus doing less. Include operational and
migration cost, not only coding convenience.

## Evolution

- Version 1:
- Trigger for the next change:
- Likely first bottleneck:
- Migration path:
- New risks introduced at the next stage:

## Validation plan

Which prototype, benchmark, failure exercise, load test, or production signal
will validate the risky assumptions?
